57:21.text: Then touched he their eyes, saying, According to your faith be it unto you.

provenance.route: Matthew 9:29 + Matthew 8:13 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “according to your faith” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and “be it unto you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse; both are Matthew 9:29, which is the whole of the sentence. “be it done unto” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Matthew 8:13's 'as thou hast believed, so be it done unto thee'. “according to thy faith” occurs in no KJV verse at all, so the possessive the Book of Mormon inflects is the one the KJV actually has.
provenance.significance: Every KJV verse standing behind this sentence is a healing. Matthew 9:29 is said to two blind men who have just answered 'Yea, Lord' to 'Believe ye that I am able to do this?'; Matthew 8:13 is said to the centurion whose servant is healed in the selfsame hour; Matthew 15:28, the third of the family, restores a daughter. Alma 57:21 puts the formula on a battlefield, and the payoff is four verses later: two hundred of the two thousand and sixty have fainted from loss of blood, 'there was not one soul of them which did perish', and not one of them is unwounded. The metalepsis is exact and it is the chapter's argument — these young men are not preserved from wounds, they are preserved through them, which is what a healing is. Note also what the tense does. Matthew's clause is an optative said before the outcome; the Book of Mormon's is an indicative said after it, and 57:21 immediately adds 'and I did remember the words which they said unto me that their mothers had taught them', so the report of the fulfilment is joined to the memory of the promise at 56:47-48.

57:21.note: 'Yea, and even according to their faith, it was done unto them.' The clause is Matthew 9:29's entire saying with the person changed from second to third and the verb realized as a past indicative, and its two halves are separately KJV singletons. The realized verb is not Matthew 9:29's own — 'be it done unto' is Matthew 8:13's — so the sentence fuses the two healing formulas of Matthew 8-9, which stand nineteen verses apart in one stretch of miracle narratives. Catalogued as a quotation on the completeness of the reproduction and the double singleton, not on length: at six words it is far below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and it is not one of his thirty-six.

57:27.text: And they were helped against them, and the Hagarites were delivered into their hand, and all that were with them: for they cried to God in the battle, and he was intreated of them; because they put their trust in him.

provenance.other: “they put their trust in him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Chronicles 5:20. The wider phrase “put their trust in” occurs in exactly six KJV verses, and the other five are all devotional rather than narrative — Psalm 2:12, 5:11, 9:10, 17:7 and Proverbs 30:5, where trusting God is praised in the abstract. 1 Chronicles 5:20 is the only place in the King James Bible where putting one's trust in God is given as the recorded cause of winning a particular battle.
provenance.significance: 1 Chronicles 5:18-22 is the KJV's one battle report constructed as an argument from faith rather than from numbers. It counts the men of war exactly (forty-four thousand seven hundred and threescore, 'valiant men, men able to bear buckler and sword'), states the enemy's losses, and then gives the cause: they cried to God in the battle, he was intreated of them, because they put their trust in him. Alma 57:25-27 is that report in the same order — the exact count of two thousand and sixty and the two hundred who fainted, the thousand slain brethren set against them, and then the cause: 'we do justly ascribe it to the miraculous power of God, because of their exceeding faith … they do put their trust in God continually.' Helaman is writing the one kind of war dispatch the King James Bible contains, and he is using its concluding formula for his own conclusion.

57:27.note: 'They are young, and their minds are firm; and they do put their trust in God continually.' The phrase is a KJV singleton in the one KJV battle narrative that ends by ascribing the victory to it, and Alma 57:26-27 is doing precisely that ascription. Held at moderate rather than high because 'put their trust in' is a live devotional idiom across the Psalms and the Book of Mormon could have taken it from there; what argues for Chronicles is not the words alone but the fact that the words arrive at the same point in the same kind of document.
